# Removing global C1 regularity from the strict-compatibility exclusion

The finite-mass proof in
`candidate ebad8045a5ec1b72`
uses only two carefully chosen boundary points of each selected anchor
fiber. They can be chosen with unique normals without assuming the entire
boundary is C1. This yields the following precise strengthening.

**Theorem.** Let d>=2 and let a finite positive actual convex fiber family
over P have strict compatibility as defined in the two-sided local-mass
note. Assume every fiber is strictly convex, with no C1 hypothesis. If
the family is an unrestricted local minimum of its maximum normalized
halfspace depth beta among positive actual families on P, then

    beta>=1/(2h(P)).                                    (1)

The only changed ingredient is the regular endpoint selection proved
below. This still does not include facets, and strict compatibility is
retained. It supplies no regularization of an arbitrary local minimum.

## 1. Radial projection preserves the required null sets

Let K be a convex body in R^d and translate a fixed interior point to
zero. Choose r,R>0 with r B_d contained in K contained in R B_d. Its
gauge g(x)=inf{t>0:x in tK} satisfies

    |g(x)-g(y)|<=|x-y|/r.

Indeed subadditivity gives g(x)-g(y)<=g(x-y)<=|x-y|/r, and exchanging
x,y gives the other direction. This does not require symmetry of K.
On the unit sphere, 1/R<=g<=1/r. Therefore rho(v)=1/g(v) is Lipschitz,
with constant at most R^2/r, and

    X(v)=rho(v)v

is Lipschitz with constant at most R+R^2/r. It maps the sphere bijectively
onto boundary K. Its inverse pi(x)=x/|x| is Lipschitz on boundary K,
with constant at most 2/r. Thus radial projection is bi-Lipschitz in the
ambient Euclidean metrics. In particular the image or preimage of a
zero H_(d-1)-measure set under these maps has zero H_(d-1)-measure.

## 2. Almost every boundary point has a unique supporting normal

Here is the precise ordinary regularity fact used. The boundary of a
convex body is locally a Lipschitz graph, and its points with more than
one supporting unit normal have H_(d-1)-measure zero.

For the graph assertion, the interior ball r B_d gives a uniform angle
with radial directions. At a boundary point x_0 let e=x_0/|x_0|. If x is
sufficiently close to x_0 and n is any supporting unit normal at x, then
n.x>=r and consequently n.e>=r/(2R). Thus the boundary near x_0 is its
upper graph in direction e, with bounded slopes, over e-perpendicular
coordinates. The graph is locally a convex or concave function, after
the appropriate orientation, and is Lipschitz. Compactness permits a
finite cover by such graph neighborhoods.

Rademacher's theorem states that a Lipschitz function on Euclidean space
is differentiable outside a Lebesgue-null set. At a differentiability
point of a convex or concave graph, all its subgradients coincide. Hence
the convex body's supporting normal there is unique. The Lipschitz graph
map takes the exceptional parameter set to an H_(d-1)-null set, and the
finite chart cover proves the assertion. This uses ordinary almost-
everywhere differentiability, not an assumption of C1 smoothness or
positive curvature.

## 3. Cap-plane boundary intersections are null under strict convexity

Suppose now that K is strictly convex. For every affine hyperplane L,

    H_(d-1)(boundary K intersect L)=0.                  (2)

If L properly cuts K, then K intersect L is a convex body in the
(d-1)-dimensional affine space L, and

    boundary K intersect L=boundary_L(K intersect L).

A convex body's boundary has zero volume in its own ambient space. One
direct proof centers an interior point at zero, observes that tD is
contained in int D for 0<t<1, and bounds its boundary measure by
|D minus tD|=(1-t^(dim D))|D|, then lets t increase to one. This proves
(2) in the proper-cut case. If L supports K, strict convexity makes
the support face at most a singleton, which has zero H_(d-1)-measure
because d>=2. An exterior plane has empty intersection.

## 4. Simultaneously regular opposite radial endpoints

Fix any finite list of cap hyperplanes and an interior point x of the
strictly convex body K. Let E be the union of their intersections with
boundary K and the boundary points without unique supporting normal.
Sections 2--3 give H_(d-1)(E)=0. After centering x at zero, Section 1
implies that pi(E) is a null subset of the unit sphere. Its antipodal
image is null as well. The sphere has positive H_(d-1)-measure, so choose

    v outside pi(E) union -pi(E).

The two radial endpoints x+rho_+(v)v and x-rho_-(v)v therefore both have
unique supporting normals and avoid every listed cap plane. Strict
convexity supplies a singleton support face for each of those normals.
Thus the individual outward hull-bump locality lemma applies at BOTH
points, while strict compatibility makes both globally exposed points.
All prescribed signed local masses from the earlier note are available.

If a listed cap passes through x, its two endpoint incidences add to one.
Giving each endpoint signed mass epsilon eta/2 makes that cap's exact
body-mass response epsilon eta/2. This is the identical finite half-mass
direction used in the preceding smooth theorem. No variation is performed
at the null exceptional set, and no limiting selection of points is needed.

## 5. Completing the local-minimum exclusion

Choose and compress the whole projected circuit groups exactly as in
`candidate ebad8045a5ec1b72`.
There are k<=h(P) relevant deepest-origin groups. Section 4 supplies the
two regular endpoints at every selected anchor, avoiding the entire finite
cap list simultaneously.

Strict convexity alone also gives equal threshold traces in every cap:
proper section areas are continuous, while supporting sections are
singletons and have zero (d-1)-volume by (2). Its own proper anchor section
provides the positive common slope. Thus all hypotheses of the exact
finite-mass cap comparison hold.

The resulting incidence matrix satisfies 0<=B_iq<=1 and B_ii=1/2.
At the local minimum its row balance yields a probability vector pi with
sum_i pi_i B_iq=beta for every selected anchor q. Hence beta>=pi_q/2.
Summing gives beta>=1/(2k)>=1/(2h(P)), proving (1).

No boundary facet was discarded: strict convexity excludes such facets
in this theorem, and d>=2 is explicitly needed for singleton supporting
sections to have zero threshold-trace measure. The exceptional null set
argument selects finitely many legitimate variation points; it is not an
almost-everywhere replacement of the final all-halfspace depth statement.
